title: ReVeal: Self-Evolving Code Agents via Reliable Self-Verification
one_liner: ReVeal trains a code agent to alternate between writing code and checking code, so long test-time improvement comes from a verifier that has learned to be dependable.
lead: Code agents often improve when they can try several drafts, run tests, inspect failures, and revise, because each cycle can remove one more source of error. The weak point is the verifier. If the agent's checks are shallow or unreliable, extra turns just wander. ReVeal trains generation and verification together, with credit assigned across turns, so the agent learns not only to write code but also to build and use checks that actually guide later revisions.

problem.h2: The problem: extra reasoning turns only help if checking is trustworthy
paras: A code agent can improve by writing a draft, running it, noticing what broke, and trying again. But many training setups reward only the final outcome. They do not directly train the checking behavior that tells the agent what to do next. As a result, the agent may produce many revisions without learning how to ask good questions about its own code.

That becomes a scaling problem at test time. If the verifier is weak, more turns do not create better search because the agent keeps revising from noisy feedback. The paper's claim is that long-horizon code improvement requires a verifier that can reliably judge partial drafts and propose tests that expose the real bug.

callout.b: The core idea in one sentence.
callout.html: Train code writing and code checking as a repeated generate-check loop, with rewards assigned across turns, so the verifier becomes useful enough to drive long test-time improvement.

panels.title: 1. First code draft fails
panels.caption: The agent writes an initial program that does not yet satisfy the task.

panels.title: 2. Weak checking gives weak guidance
panels.viz_args: Only final pass/fail reward -> little guidance on which revision mattered
panels.caption: Outcome-only feedback does not explain which turn improved the program.

panels.title: 3. ReVeal runs a verification turn
panels.caption: The agent constructs tests, runs tools, and checks the current draft.

panels.title: 4. Credit flows to the useful turn
panels.caption: Turn-level credit tells training which verification action actually helped later success.

panels.title: 5. Code keeps improving across many turns
panels.caption: A stronger verifier supports longer revision chains because each new turn has better evidence.

steps.text: The agent writes code for the task, just as a normal code model would.
Instead of stopping at the first draft, the agent builds checks, runs tools, and inspects the behavior of the program so that it can learn what is wrong.

steps.b: Step 3: Assign credit to each turn
steps.text: The training setup attributes reward at the turn level, so useful verification actions receive positive learning signal because they enabled a later repair.

steps.b: Step 4: Revise code using the check results
steps.text: The next generation step uses the evidence gathered during verification to fix the program more precisely.

steps.b: Step 5: Repeat beyond the training horizon
steps.text: At test time the agent can continue this loop for many more turns than seen in training, because the verification behavior itself has become dependable enough to guide the longer search.

object.h2: What changes: the unit of training becomes a turn pair
paras: The central object is no longer a single code sample with one final reward. It is a sequence of generation and verification turns. Each verification step creates information that later turns can act on, so the training signal has to treat those steps as consequential decisions rather than as hidden internal chatter.

hidden.name: How often a check points the search in the right direction
paras: The decisive hidden quantity is not just whether a test fails. It is whether the verification step gives information that helps the next revision move toward a correct program because it isolates the real source of error. A bad test can fail for the wrong reason, or a vague check can say that something is wrong without locating the source. In both cases, extra turns add little value.

ReVeal tries to improve this hidden quantity directly. By rewarding helpful verification turns, it pushes the agent toward tests and tool uses that expose the actual mistake instead of producing noisy signals.

heat.caption: Darker cells are checks with higher value because they produce evidence that can drive the next repair.

reads.html: A good check tells the agent what to fix next, not just that the current draft is bad.
Reliable self-verification is the source of useful test-time scaling because later turns only help when their evidence improves the next revision.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: better checks create a better search process
paras: The method works because code repair is a search problem over many candidate programs. Search improves only when each step uses evidence that narrows the remaining error because that evidence eliminates some wrong repair directions. ReVeal makes verification a trained skill, so the agent learns to create targeted tests and read tool feedback in a way that guides revision.

Turn-level credit is important because the final pass or fail may occur several turns after the key decision. If one verification turn exposed the real bug and a later generation turn fixed it, both decisions deserve credit. Training them together produces a code agent whose later revisions are grounded in stronger evidence, which is why the paper can extend to many more turns at test time than were seen during training, because the later turns now start from more dependable checks.

stages.s: Assign turn-level reward to useful checks
Longer test-time improvement because each later turn uses stronger checks

math.h2: The training signal: sum reward across turns
math.words: A simple view is to score the whole trajectory by adding the value contributed by each generation turn and each verification turn. The goal is not merely to maximize final success, but to strengthen intermediate actions that make later success more likely.
symbols: the learning signal for the code-writing action at turn t
the learning signal for the checking action at turn t
the total signal over the full revision process

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Turn 1 writes code that almost works but mishandles empty input.
Turn 2 creates a boundary-case test for empty input and exposes the exact bug.
Turn 3 fixes the bug and the program passes.
If the final success gives reward 1, the useful boundary-case test should receive some of that credit because it created the evidence for the repair.
ReVeal trains this way so that future runs learn to create the same kind of useful checks.

math.note: The important change is that verification actions become first-class learning targets, not mere side effects of generation.

bars.h2: The payoff: more turns stay productive

charts.title: Outcome-only training
charts.note: Without explicit training for verification, later turns often repeat weak checks or noisy rewrites.

charts.title: ReVeal
charts.note: The paper reports stronger Pass@k and continued improvement past 20 turns on LiveCodeBench because the verifier keeps producing evidence that helps later drafts.

items.html: If the verification turn only runs easy cases, the system may overfit to tests that do not reveal the real bug.
If rewards cannot distinguish which turn helped, useful verification behavior may not improve even after many trajectories because the learning signal never points clearly to the valuable check.
A strong test still fails if the agent draws the wrong conclusion from the output. Good verification requires both useful checks and correct interpretation.

items.b: Done right: later turns remain informative.
items.html: The method succeeds when each new round of checking reduces uncertainty enough that the next code revision is more targeted than the previous one.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a set of small programming tasks with hidden edge cases. Train one agent on final pass-or-fail only, and train another on a generate-check loop with explicit reward for verification turns. At test time allow both agents many revision turns on fresh tasks so that the evaluation can reveal whether the extra turns stay useful. Record how often each turn adds a useful test or bug hypothesis, and how often the final program passes. The demo should show that the second agent benefits from extra turns because its checks sharpen later revisions, while the first agent often spends those turns on low-value rewrites.
demo.metric_eq: Useful-turn rate = (# turns that create evidence leading to a later fix) / (total verification turns).
demo.closing: The demo must show that the gain comes from a better checking process because the rewarded verifier produces stronger evidence, not merely from allowing more retries.
